item.title: Meta's Troubling History with User Privacy
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
Letting Meta lead the charge on superintelligence, huh? It's a good thing they have a responsible and trustworthy track record, right? Well, think again:

**2025:**

- Meta secretly tracked Android users' browsing through hidden methods and settled a $1.4 billion lawsuit in Texas over biometric data collection without consent.

**2024:**

- The EU investigated Meta for issues related to child safety, false advertising, and data privacy.
- Forty-two U.S. states sued Meta for utilizing addictive algorithms that harm minors.
- The FTC accused Meta of breaching privacy rules, particularly concerning teenagers.

**2023:**

- Fined €1.2 billion by Ireland for illegal data transfers to the U.S. (GDPR violation).
- Health data leaks were revealed through the Meta Pixel.
- Fined €405 million for inadequate data protection for children on Instagram.
- Fined €390 million for enforcing personalized ads.

**2022:**

- A data breach exposed information of 533 million users, resulting in a €265 million fine.
- Settled for $725 million over the secret sharing of user data, including with Cambridge Analytica.

**2021:**

- Paid $650 million to settle claims regarding facial recognition privacy violations.

**2019:**

- The FTC fined Meta $5 billion for privacy violations, and the SEC $100 million for misleading investors.

**2018:**

- Cambridge Analytica misused data from up to 87 million users.
- A bug exposed details of 29 million users, leading to a €251 million fine.
- Hackers compromised 90 million accounts due to a vulnerability.

**2013–2018:**

- Meta shared user data with over 150 companies without clear consent.
- Early bugs exposed millions of users' contact information.

**Ongoing Issues:**

- Tracks non-users through "shadow profiles."
- Records location information even when it's disabled.
- WhatsApp privacy policy changes triggered backlash.
- Facebook conducted non-consensual psychological experiments.

It's important to remember that Big Tech prioritizes business, profits, government relations, and self-serving interests over the well-being of users. These companies are not benevolent.

item.title: China's AI Sports Bots: A Cover for Military Innovation
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
I recently had an intriguing discussion with Perplexity where I made the intuitive connection that China’s humanoid AI sports bots might serve as a cover for testing real-time decision-making and athletic skills for future battlefield scenarios. This may provide them an edge in the ongoing, unspoken AI cold war between the US and China that is characterized by the development and weaponization of ever-advancing AI systems, which we can see are now beginning to take physical form.

Perplexity confirmed my suspicions (to an extent) and I felt it was a clever rouse. The irony, however, is that they're developing these technologies in the name of safety. Their public pitch is that they're testing these technologies to ensure safe human/AI interactions in the future.

Framing a false initiative for disguised intentions as such is, of course, not unique to China; however, at least they're having some fun competition in the process. Unlike the US, which has a history of falsely framing another nation as a hostile threat when in reality they likely only threaten US business interests.

Continue to spread awareness my fellow devs. Keep the torch of truth bright and burning, and we may yet have an impact on whether the AI age will be mankind’s greatest achievement or worst nightmare.

#ai safety and ethics first

#for future generations

#for societal stability

#for our continued existence

#don’t trust big tech

item.title: Privacy Policy
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
Who we are

Our website address is: https://mistykmedia.com.

Comments

When visitors leave comments on the site, we collect the data shown in the comments form, and also the visitor’s IP address and browser user agent string to help with spam detection.

An anonymized string created from your email address (also called a hash) is provided to the Gravatar service to see if you are using it. The Gravatar service privacy policy is available here: https://automattic.com/privacy/. After approval of your comment, your profile picture is visible to the public in the context of your comment.

Media

If you upload images to the website, you should avoid uploading images with embedded location data (EXIF GPS) included. Visitors to the website can download and extract any location data from images on the website.

Cookies

If you leave a comment on our site, you may opt in to saving your name, email address, and website in cookies. These are for your convenience so that you do not have to fill in your details again when you leave another comment. These cookies will last for one year.

If you visit our login page, we will set a temporary cookie to determine if your browser accepts cookies. This cookie contains no personal data and is discarded when you close your browser.

When you log in, we will also set up several cookies to save your login information and your screen display choices. Login cookies last for two days, and screen options cookies last for a year. If you select "Remember Me", your login will persist for two weeks. If you log out of your account, the login cookies will be removed.

If you edit or publish an article, an additional cookie will be saved in your browser. This cookie includes no personal data and simply indicates the post ID of the article you just edited. It expires after 1 day.

Embedded content from other websites

Articles on this site include embedded content (e.g., videos, images, articles, etc.). Embedded content from other websites behaves in the same way as if the visitor had visited the other website.

These websites collect data about you, use cookies, embed additional third-party tracking, and monitor your interaction with that embedded content, including tracking your interaction with the embedded content if you have an account and are logged in to that website.

Who we share your data with

If you request a password reset, your IP address will be included in the reset email.

How long do we retain your data?

If you leave a comment, the comment and its metadata are retained indefinitely. This is so we can recognize and approve any follow-up comments automatically instead of holding them in a moderation queue.

For users who register on our website (if any), we also store the personal information they provide in their user profile. All users can see, edit, or delete their personal information at any time (except they cannot change their username). Website administrators can also see and edit that information.

What rights do you have over your data?

If you have an account on this site or have left comments, you can request to receive an exported file of the personal data we hold about you, including any data you have provided to us. You can also request that we erase any personal data we hold about you. This does not include any data we are obliged to keep for administrative, legal, or security purposes.

Where your data is sent

Visitor comments may be checked through an automated spam detection service.

item.title: Project 2025: Pt. 1 - The Heritage Foundation
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
Project 2025 Series, Part One: The Institutional Origins of Project 2025 and The Heritage Foundation

Introduction to the Series

This essay is the first in a three-part series about Project 2025. It looks at where the project came from, its policy ideas, and why it matters in today’s American politics. In this section, the focus is on the history of the Heritage Foundation, the main conservative policy group linked to Project 2025, and how it fits into the rise of modern conservative organizations in the United States. Britannica Project 2025

The Powell Memorandum and the Expansion of Conservative Institutional Strategy

To understand the political environment that led to the Heritage Foundation, it helps to start with a 1971 memo by Lewis F. Powell Jr. to Eugene B. Sydnor Jr. of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Called “Attack on American Free Enterprise System,” the memo said the American economic system was under steady criticism from some academics, the media, and public-interest groups. Powell urged business leaders to respond with more organized and long-term efforts. While experts disagree on how much the memo influenced subsequent events, it is often seen as a key call for a stronger conservative, pro-business network. Washington and Lee University School of Law Scholarly Commons
The Powell Memorandum is important not just because it may have prompted later changes, but also because it introduced a new strategy. The memo stressed the need to influence groups that shape public opinion, law, and policy. Afterward, more conservative organizations appeared and grew, with the Heritage Foundation becoming one of the most well-known. Washington and Lee University School of Law Scholarly Commons Britannica
The Heritage Foundation as a Policy Institution
The Heritage Foundation started in 1973. Britannica calls it a conservative policy research group in Washington, D.C., founded by congressional aides Edwin Feulner and Paul Weyrich. Heritage says it was created to give Congress research and arguments for conservative ideas. These details show that Heritage was meant to focus on policy and government, not on building a large membership. Britannica The Heritage Foundation
This setup helps explain why Heritage has stayed influential for so long. Instead of primarily focusing on getting out the vote, Heritage focused on producing research, advice, and policy plans for lawmakers, government officials, and the media. Heritage says its work includes briefings, testimony, media outreach, and the development of conservative ideas into concrete policy proposals. No matter your view of the group, its approach has always aimed at shaping policy and government decisions. The Heritage Foundation Britannica

Paul Weyrich and Conservative Movement-Building

Paul Weyrich is known as a key figure in the rise of the American New Right. Britannica lists him as a co-founder of the Heritage Foundation, and later writers have highlighted his work in building a wider network of conservative groups. Weyrich matters not just as a founder but as someone who helped create lasting organizations that could shape policy, media stories, and long-term political goals.  Britannica Crisis Magazine
Looking at organizations, Weyrich’s main insight was that political influence is about more than just campaigns and elections. Think tanks, advocacy groups, training, and networks of experts can shape which policies future leaders choose. Heritage became one of the best examples of this approach.  Crisis Magazine Britannica

Edwin J. Feulner and Institutional Consolidation

While Weyrich shaped Heritage’s strategy, Edwin Feulner was key to ensuring the organization's longevity. Heritage lists Feulner as a founding trustee from 1973 to 2025 and as president from 1977 to 2013. During his tenure as leader, he helped build a national network of conservative policy groups and improved Heritage's ability to provide practical policy advice.  The Heritage Foundation
Feulner’s role in Heritage’s history is clear when one looks at how the group operated. With him in charge, Heritage became known for producing timely policy briefs and broader government plans. Heritage’s own reviews highlight how it became more important to presidents, Congress, and the media. This is part of why the group stood out during Republican administrations, especially starting with Reagan.  The Heritage Foundation Britannica

Joseph Coors and the Role of Donor Support

Heritage’s early growth also relied on financial support. According to Philanthropy Roundtable, Joseph Coors believed conservatives needed their own think tanks, so he wrote a $250,000 check in 1972 to help start the Heritage Foundation. The same source says Coors’s support was a turning point and that he kept funding the group over the years.  Philanthropy Roundtable
Coors’s role matters beyond the founding of Heritage. It shows how think tanks rely on donors and philanthropy to keep going and expand their influence. For Heritage, this support helped it stay active and shape conservative policy for many years. Recent reports also highlight that wealthy donors continue to support groups linked to Project 2025. For instance, DeSmog reported that the Adolph Coors Foundation funded several Project 2025 advisory groups from 2020 to 2023. While that report is investigative journalism rather than official documentation, it still shows current funding trends related to Project 2025.  Philanthropy Roundtable DeSmog

From Mandate for Leadership to Project 2025

A good example of Heritage’s long-term strategy is its Mandate for Leadership series. Heritage says its 1980 Mandate for Leadership became a key policy guide for the Reagan administration, and Britannica also notes that President Reagan used Heritage’s handbook for advice. No matter how you view these claims, they show that Heritage has always aimed to shape not just debate, but actual government decisions.  The Heritage Foundation Britannica
Project 2025 is a modern version of that earlier approach. Heritage describes it as a large coalition with four main parts: a policy agenda, staffing, training, and a 180-day plan. Heritage also said the project now has 100 coalition partners, showing how large the network is. The main policy document, Mandate for Leadership 2025: The Conservative Promise, is a long handbook—about 900 pages—meant to guide a future conservative administration.  The Heritage Foundation Project 2025 PDF
Seen in historical perspective, Project 2025 is less a sudden development than the continuation of a longstanding institutional practice. The same organization that developed policy handbooks for earlier Republican administrations has now paired a modern policy volume with a personnel pipeline, a training program, and a transition-planning structure. That combination suggests a more systematic attempt to connect ideology, staffing, and administrative execution.  The Heritage Foundation Britannica

Conclusion

The historical origins of Project 2025 are best understood through the development of the institutions behind it. The Powell Memorandum reflected a broader call for sustained institutional engagement by business and conservative actors. The Heritage Foundation emerged in 1973 as a policy-focused organization intended to supply research and recommendations to political decision-makers. Paul Weyrich helped articulate the value of institution-building, Edwin Feulner helped transform Heritage into an enduring policy organization, and Joseph Coors provided important early financial support.  Washington and Lee University School of Law Scholarly Commons - The Heritage Foundation Philanthropy Roundtable
From this perspective, Project 2025 is not simply a contemporary policy document. It is the product of a longer organizational tradition in which conservative institutions seek to shape governance through research, donor support, personnel development, and administrative planning. Understanding that institutional history is essential for evaluating the project itself, which will be the focus of the next part of this series.  Britannica The Heritage Foundation

item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded: This haunting question has been gnawing at me with increasing severity ever since I was a young child. Since the age of about 6 or so, I've dealt with a lurking feeling of dread and impending doom that seemed to whisper in the hallway echoes of my primary school. Much of this can be owed to the unfortunate fact that my sense of childhood innocence and wonder were but too brief as they were quickly extinguished and supplanted with not only traumas of varying degrees, but with the introduction to and wrestling with concepts that could challenge and leave grown adults shifting in their seats.

item.content:encoded: Money, Power, and the Empathy Drop-Off As we examine the rather tumultuous state of human affairs in 2026, it's hard not to wonder, "Why does it seem as though everyday ordinary working and middle-class folks, such as our friends, family, and neighbors are, for the most part, kind, caring, compassionate, at times even self-sacrificing and courageous. But if we zoom out a bit, the world around is chaotic, messy, heartbreaking, corrupt, and in certain parts quite literally on fire?" Now a classical model of modern psychology, such as a Freudian explanation might tell us that international hostilities and humanity's alarmingly consistent state of agression, hostility, and armed conflict the same contour keeps reappearing: as wealth and social status climb, empathy and ordinary kindness tend to atrophy, while entitlement, narcissism, and a flexible relationship with ethics intensify. The claim is not that money turns everyone cruel—only that prosperity re-engineers the surrounding incentives, quietly rewarding self-focus unless institutions or communities actively push the other way. Researchers usually proxy “wealth” via socioeconomic status, folding together income, education, occupation, and how people perceive their own class position. When these variables are tested against measures of generosity, compassion, and moral choice, the data draw a familiar curve: people lower on the socioeconomic ladder prove more attuned to others and more likely to lend help; those higher up reliably score higher on entitlement scales, narcissistic self-importance, and willingness to bend rules when the cost-benefit math favors them. Wealth, Empathy, and Compassion One of the cleanest lines of evidence comes from Paul Piff and colleagues, who ran a series of experiments testing how social class predicts prosocial behavior. In economic games and lab tasks, lower-class participants were more generous, more charitable, more trusting, and more likely to help strangers than higher-class participants—even though they had fewer resources to spare. Follow‑up analyses showed that this wasn’t just “nice poor people” mythology; the effect was mediated by stronger egalitarian values and higher feelings of compassion among lower-class participants. In another set of studies, researchers showed that social class is differentially associated with types of positive emotion: upper‑class people report more self‑oriented emotions like pride and contentment, while lower‑class people report more other‑oriented emotions like compassion, love, and awe. That maps nicely onto your initial notes: when your life circumstances force you to rely on others and constantly read the room, you get very good at perspective‑taking; when you’re buffered by money and status, the emotional spotlight tends to turn inward. A chapter literally called “The Class–Compassion Gap” pulls all this together: it argues that upper‑class contexts foster self-focus, reduced attention to others, and lower compassion, while lower‑class contexts foster interdependence and heightened attunement to others’ distress. This is consistent with broader reviews on social class and prosocial behavior, which find a robust pattern of lower-class individuals giving more, helping more, and sharing more in controlled experiments, despite living with more threat and uncertainty. From Compassion to Conduct: When Wealth Loosens the Rules The empathy gap is one side of the story; the behavioral side is equally ugly. A famous series of seven studies in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that upper‑class participants were more likely to break traffic laws, cut off other drivers, ignore pedestrians, lie in negotiations, cheat to win prizes, and endorse unethical workplace behavior than lower‑class participants. These weren’t tiny effects: in field observations, drivers of higher‑status cars were several times more likely to cut off other vehicles at intersections and to blow through crosswalks while a pedestrian was waiting. Crucially, this wasn’t just “because they can afford the ticket.” When the researchers primed any participants—rich or poor—to endorse greed as a positive value, their willingness to behave unethically increased; and upper‑class people spontaneously held more favorable attitudes toward greed to begin with. In other words, the social meaning of wealth—freedom, independence, being above constraint—seems to loosen internal guardrails around fairness and honesty. Qualitative and popular-science syntheses of this work repeat the same theme: as wealth and status increase, altruistic behavior and everyday ethical restraint often decrease, unless people deliberately cultivate countervailing values. Emotional well‑being doesn’t keep rising with income forever either—there’s evidence that happiness plateaus and sometimes gives way to feelings of emptiness or disconnection once material needs are easily met, which can further reinforce self‑focused coping strategies. The Power Paradox and the “Rich Brain” This is where Dacher Keltner’s “power paradox” comes in. Keltner’s work shows that people often gain power because they’re socially intelligent, empathic, and good at reading others—but once they have power, those same capacities start to erode. Over twenty years of experiments, his group found that people under the influence of power become more impulsive, less risk‑aware, and worse at seeing things from someone else’s point of view. Neuroscientist Sukhvinder Obhi added a literal brain‑level layer: using transcranial magnetic stimulation, his team found that powerful individuals showed reduced activation in neural “mirroring” processes, which are thought to underpin our ability to simulate and empathize with others’ experiences. Other studies Keltner cites show that powerful people become less likely to mimic others’ facial expressions or body language—subtle behaviors that help create emotional resonance and empathy in everyday interactions. Popular summaries of this work are blunt: power can act “like a traumatic brain injury,” dampening the exact neural and behavioral systems that helped you earn people’s trust in the first place. That maps directly onto your point about power and perspective‑taking; the more resources and control you accumulate, the easier it becomes—neurologically and behaviorally—to stop tracking the inner life of anyone outside your immediate interests. Life in an Epistemic Bubble You also flagged something that’s less clinical but just as important: extreme wealth physically removes people from everyday reality. Sociologists and philosophers describe related structures as “epistemic bubbles” and “echo chambers”—environments where relevant voices are either absent or actively discredited. In an epistemic bubble, you simply don’t encounter information that challenges you; in an echo chamber, you’ve also been trained to distrust any outsider who tries. Most of the academic work on epistemic bubbles focuses on politics and social media, but the architecture is basically identical to elite life: gated communities, private jets, VIP lines, concierge medicine, and a staff whose job security depends on making your day go smoothly. Philosophers like C. Thi Nguyen argue that these structures create “impaired informational topologies”—networks with poor connectivity to dissenting perspectives, which encourages increasingly extreme and self‑reinforcing worldviews. This helps explain cost-blindness and the surreal advice you sometimes hear from the ultra‑rich (“Just move for a better job,” “Why don’t they get a tutor?”). If you haven’t had to think about rent, copays, or overdraft fees in twenty years, resource constraints eventually feel like a weird theoretical artifact rather than the primary operating condition of most human lives. Combine that insulation with the reduced mirroring and perspective‑taking we just talked about, and you start to get an elite psychology that’s not just selfish, but genuinely out of touch. Dark Triad Traits: Who Rises to the Top? Now we get to the “chicken or egg” part: are wealthy elites more narcissistic and psychopathic because money corrupts them, or because those traits helped them get rich to begin with? Research on the “Dark Triad”—narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy—suggests the answer is “both, interacting over time.” A literature review on cognitive empathy and the Dark Triad finds a consistent pattern: Machiavellianism and psychopathy are strongly associated with reduced empathy—especially affective empathy—while narcissism has a more complex profile, with some cognitive empathy preserved or even heightened in certain subtypes. A recent meta‑analysis titled “Cold hearts and dark minds” confirms this: psychopathy and Machiavellianism show significant empathy deficits, while narcissism often involves impaired emotional resonance but relatively intact perspective‑taking that can be used for self‑enhancement or manipulation. These traits show up non‑trivially in business and leadership contexts. Reviews of “corporate psychopathy” argue that individuals with subclinical psychopathic traits—fearlessness, lack of remorse, charm, manipulativeness, low anxiety—are overrepresented in positions of power where there are large financial rewards and weak constraints, such as finance, corporate banking, and certain executive roles. These individuals can appear charismatic and decisive in the short term but are associated with higher rates of fraud, organizational dysfunction, and long‑term damage once the metrics catch up. More recent work on leadership and the Dark Triad suggests that people high in these traits are disproportionately drawn to roles promising authority, status, and control. Popular and clinical commentary on the “billionaire class” echoes this: extreme wealth and elite networks create a perfect habitat for dark‑triad individuals to thrive, because traits like ruthlessness, callousness, and strategic manipulation are rewarded rather than punished.   Wealth as Narcissism Fuel On the socialization side, there’s now explicit evidence that higher social class is associated with more entitlement and narcissism. A paper literally titled “Wealth and the inflated self” found that upper‑class individuals reported greater psychological entitlement and narcissistic tendencies across five studies, and were more likely to behave narcissistically (e.g., choosing to look at themselves in a mirror when given the option). When researchers experimentally induced egalitarian values in upper‑class participants, their narcissism scores dropped to match those of lower‑class peers, suggesting these differences are at least somewhat malleable. Paul Piff has summarized this body of work bluntly: as income and status go up, self-focus, entitlement, and belief in one’s own deservingness tend to increase, while empathy and concern for others’ well‑being tend to fall. That shift in self‑narrative has political and moral consequences; upper‑class people who feel more deserving often favor policies that lock in their advantages, like lower taxes and reduced social spending, even when the economic benefits to them are marginal compared to the harm for everyone else. Narcissism research adds an interesting twist: people with narcissistic personality traits often have intact cognitive empathy but impaired affective empathy—meaning they can accurately understand what others feel without actually sharing those feelings. One review on narcissistic personality disorder describes “affective dissonance,” where awareness of others’ emotions coexists with cold or exploitative behavior, especially in more antagonistic “rivalry” forms of narcissism. Put a person like that into a wealth and power environment that constantly rewards self‑aggrandizement, and you essentially have a narcissism feedback loop: the world keeps telling you that you really are as special and deserving as you always suspected. Psychopathy, Pain, and Compassion Psychopathy is its own beast, but there are some relevant nuances. Clinical psychopathy is rare in the general population, but subclinical psychopathic traits—especially egocentricity, callousness, and antisociality—vary dimensionally and show up more often in certain high‑stakes occupations. A recent study on pain sensitivity found that reduced sensitivity to one’s own pain mediated the link between psychopathic traits and diminished empathy for others’ pain, suggesting a shared mechanism that helps explain why harming others doesn’t register as strongly. Another study on subclinical psychopathy and compassion found that psychopathic traits blunt the effects of compassion‑inducing interventions: people high in egocentricity and callousness were less responsive to attempts to ramp up self‑ or other‑compassion. That matters in a wealth context because compassion—especially toward those structurally below you—is a key brake on exploiting others for gain. If someone already has muted compassion and they enter a system that rewards ruthless optimization, the guardrails are basically gone. Meta‑analytic work on the Dark Triad reinforces the “cold hearts” picture: psychopathy and Machiavellianism are consistently linked with affective empathy deficits, while narcissism is more mixed but often involves using cognitive empathy instrumentally. This dovetails with the corporate psychopathy literature showing that leaders high in these traits can be superficially charming, strategically smart, and devastatingly destructive to human beings and institutions over time.   Selection vs. Socialization: The Feedback Loop So which comes first—dark traits or big bank accounts? The honest answer is that we’re looking at a reinforcing loop. On the selection side, people higher in narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathic traits are more likely to seek out high‑status, high‑power roles because those environments match their craving for dominance, control, and recognition. Studies of career preferences and leadership styles show that dark‑triad traits are associated with a stronger attraction to hierarchical, competitive, and zero‑sum environments—exactly the sort of domains (finance, corporate leadership, certain corners of politics) that generate disproportionate wealth. On the socialization side, wealth and power act like an amplifier. Once you’re in an elite position, you’re surrounded by people who depend on your favor, your failures are often externalized (“the market,” “bad staff”), and you live inside the epistemic bubble we talked about earlier. Keltner’s power paradox and Obhi’s mirroring work suggest that just being in a position of power slowly dulls the neural and behavioral systems responsible for empathy and perspective‑taking, even if you didn’t start out particularly callous. You pointed to the likely cycle, and the research basically agrees: reduced empathy and elevated narcissism make aggressive, self‑interested wealth‑maximizing decisions easier; those decisions generate more power and resources; that power further erodes empathy and inflates the sense of being special and separate. Over years and decades, you can end up with extremely rich individuals who sincerely believe their fortune is purely self‑made and morally deserved, while being almost neurologically and socially insulated from the feedback that might challenge that story.   Detachment from “Everyday Reality” The structural detachment piece is less lab‑measurable but heavily theorized. Philosophers and social epistemologists describe how epistemic bubbles and echo chambers distort people’s ability to learn from the world: bubbles by omission of alternative perspectives, echo chambers by teaching members to distrust any outside sources. These structures have been tied to the rise of populist and authoritarian politics, where leaders actively promote group norms that filter information through identity and loyalty rather than accuracy. Translate that into class terms: if everyone you interact with is staff, advisors, or peers who share your material insulation, the feedback you get about reality is heavily curated. Mistakes get hidden, dissent gets self‑censored, and most importantly, the lived experience of ordinary constraints—waiting rooms, late fees, public schools, public transport—simply disappears from your day‑to‑day data stream. Over time, that creates a kind of sincere cluelessness: not cartoon cruelty, but a genuine inability to model what life is like for people who don’t share your buffers. This is where some of the more infuriating elite commentary comes from: policy suggestions that assume infinite mobility, infinite slack, and infinite resilience in populations that have none of those things. If your own life has been a long string of “risks” protected by parental money, elite networks, and soft landings, the fact that other people’s risks end in homelessness or prison never really lands as a meaningful possibility.   Caveats, Biases, and the “Not All Rich People” Clause A few important caveats, because nuance actually matters here. First, these are statistical tendencies, not destiny. There are many wealthy individuals who retain high empathy, give away substantial portions of their wealth, and use their status to push for more egalitarian policies; the social-class literature even notes that class differences in narcissism and entitlement can be reduced by priming egalitarian values or reminding people of interdependence. The same studies that implicate wealth in unethical behavior also show that attitudes toward greed and explicit moral norms moderate the effect. Second, most of this research uses perceived social class, not just income or net worth. Someone from a working‑class background who becomes wealthy may carry different emotional templates than someone born into a dynasty, even if they end up at similar SES levels on paper. Reviews on inequality emphasize that early‑life conditions—stability, security, exposure to threat—shape later responses to power, sometimes making formerly poor elites more sensitive to injustice, and sometimes pushing them into hyper‑meritocratic “I did it, so can you” narratives that erase structural barriers. Third, there’s a status bias in how we label traits. The same behavior that gets called “narcissistic” or “antisocial” in poor or marginalized people is often reframed as “visionary,” “disruptive,” or “tough‑minded” in CEOs and politicians. Corporate psychopathy researchers explicitly warn that charming, high‑functioning psychopaths can be rewarded and promoted for years before the damage they cause is recognized, while people lower in the hierarchy get pathologized and punished for much milder versions of the same traits. Finally, some scholars point out that the “upper class = bad, lower class = good” story can be oversimplified. Reviews caution that effects vary by culture, measurement method, and context, and they call for more nuanced models that incorporate ideology, social norms, and institutional design. Still, even the cautious reviews don’t dispute the core pattern you’re interested in: wealth and power tend to nudge humans toward lower compassion, higher entitlement, and a greater tolerance for exploiting others—unless something actively pushes back.   Taken together, the research backs your core intuition: there is a real, evidence‑based link between amassing large amounts of wealth and resources and exhibiting more narcissistic, callous, and ethically flexible traits—but it emerges from a system of selection, amplification, and structural insulation, not a simple “rich = evil” switch. Dark‑triad tendencies make certain people unusually good at playing ruthless games; those games pay extremely well; the winnings then further erode empathy and detach the winners from the consequences of their own decisions. This is the throughline: the system is practically designed to elevate people with low empathy, feed their narcissism, protect them from reality, and then call the whole thing “merit.”   Sources   matrix.berkeley doi.apa pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih en.wikipedia academic.oup vcresearch.berkeley marginalrevolution studyfinds dataofplano huxley sciencefocus philarchive academic.oup linkinghub.elsevier pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih inc pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih reed pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih repository.tcu academyoflifeplanning dataofplano huxley cambridge academic.oup doi.apa experts.illinois linkinghub.elsevier

item.title: Human Beats AI in 10-Hour Coding Marathon – Here’s How
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
In a moment straight out of a tech-thriller, the competitive programming world witnessed an epic upset: Przemysław Dębiak—better known as “Psyho”—defeated OpenAI’s cutting-edge AI in a grueling 10-hour coding marathon at the AtCoder World Tour Finals 2025. Facing off against a powerful machine opponent, Debiak showed that human grit and ingenuity still pack a punch.

The Showdown in Tokyo

Held in Tokyo, Japan, the AtCoder World Tour Finals 2025 brought together 12 of the world’s best programmers for a marathon-style Heuristic Contest. The challenge: solve a complex optimization problem involving robots navigating grids.

In an unprecedented twist, OpenAI entered the competition with its AI system, “OpenAIAHC,” setting up a true man-versus-machine showdown that had everyone watching.

The Final Score

As the clock wound down, OpenAIAHC held a narrow lead. But in the final stretch, Debiak executed a stunning strategic surge, overtaking the AI and clinching victory in dramatic fashion.

The How and Why?

Debiak’s win was nothing short of incredible and a true demonstration in human problem-solving abilities. His instincts, sharpened by years of high-level competition, guided him through the chaos of the challenge. While the AI rapidly cranked out solutions, Debiak crafted a unique and creative approach that made the difference. And through it all, he showed remarkable endurance, relying on experience and a heavy dose of caffeine to push through exhaustion.

Afterward, he summed it up candidly: “I’m completely exhausted… I got about 10 hours of sleep in three days. I’m barely alive. Humanity has prevailed.”

Looking Ahead

With AI evolving at breakneck speed, many believe this may likely be the last time a human claims the top spot in such a contest. Even OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, from atop his AI/Tech throne gave a rare gesture of approval.

Just a year ago, no AI even cracked the top 10. Now, OpenAI’s model came within 10% of winning. The speed of progress is staggering—and if I may be frank—a little spooky.

Who Is “Psyho”?

Przemysław Debiak is no stranger to elite competition. A four-time TopCoder Open Marathon champion and a key contributor to OpenAI Five, the AI that beat professional Dota 2 players. He’s earned a reputation for unmatched creativity and endurance in high-pressure coding arenas.

The Bigger Picture

As AI tools grow smarter and faster, human creativity, instinct, and resilience still matter—and for now, they still win. But the question looms: how long can we hold the line?

OpenAI’s remark: “Congrats to the champion for holding us off this time.”

Let me know in the comments if you think machine or man will be next year's victor.

If you enjoyed this, then consider sharing or subscribing.

-Mistyk

item.title: Trump's Crypto Empire: From White House to Wallet
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
Trump's Crypto Empire

 

Trump's net worth has ballooned to around $5.5 billion as of 2025, and get this – about 60% of that ($3.3 billion) comes straight from cryptocurrency. Yeah, the guy who once called Bitcoin a “scam” is now the cryptocurrency poster child. It's like watching your grandpa discover TikTok and suddenly go viral.

 

From White House to Wallet

 

The show's star is World Liberty Financial, a DeFi platform Trump launched in September 2024. Official disclosures show he pocketed $57.4 million from it in 2024 alone. The Trump family owns 60% and snags 75% of revenue from token sales. By July 2025, they'd raised over $550 million in private sales, funneling an estimated $390 million to the family coffers. Oh, and they scooped up 73,600 Ethereum tokens worth $275 million. Not bad for a side hustle while running the free world.

 

Trump's $TRUMP Meme Coin

 

Then there's the infamous $TRUMP meme coin, dropped right before his second inauguration in January 2025. It skyrocketed to a $27 billion market cap, valuing Trump's slice at over $20 billion. But here's the dry humor part: while Trump & Co. raked in $100 million in trading fees, 813,294 wallets lost a collective $2 billion. Only 58 wallets walked away with over $10 million each, totaling $1.1 billion in profits. Analysts call it a textbook pump-and-dump – because nothing says “presidential” like a coin that evaporates retail investors' savings faster than you can say “you're fired.”

 

Insider Trading Shenanigans: Tariffs, Tweets, and Timely Trades Now

 

It is also suspected that Trump may be committing insider trading based on the suspicious circumstances of these massive financial gains. Picture this: April 9, 2025, 9:37 AM. Trump tweets on Truth Social: “THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!! DJT.” Four hours later? He announces a 90-day pause on his massive tariffs. Stocks surge 9.5%, adding $4 trillion to the market. That's one hell of a coincidence. Investigations uncovered some eyebrow-raising patterns: Over 90% of stock sales by top Trump officials happened in 10-day windows before big tariff announcements. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Dan Scavino dumped up to $5 million in Trump Media stock the day before the April reveal. Mysterious traders bet big on market rebounds via zero-day options right before the news dropped. Even Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene scooped up $21,000 to $315,000 in stocks on April 8–9.

 

Democrats aren't letting this slide. Senator Adam Schiff and Rep. Ruben Gallego are demanding probes, Elizabeth Warren calls it “corruption in plain sight,” and the House Committee on Financial Services dubbed it “the world's biggest market manipulation scheme.” It's like insider trading, but with extra presidential flair – because why trade on whispers when you can shout from the Oval Office?

 

Beyond Crypto

 

The Business Bonanza During Office Hours, Trump's money-making didn't stop at digital coins. During his first term (2017–2021), his businesses pulled in $2.4 billion in revenue, including $1.6 billion in outside income. Foreign governments chipped in too – at least $7.8 million from 20 countries over two years, violating the Foreign Emoluments Clause. China led with $5.5 million, followed by Saudi Arabia ($615,422) and Qatar ($465,744). No congressional approval? No problem, apparently.

 

Fast-forward to term two: No ethics pledge for the administration (breaking 50 years of tradition), exclusive dinners for $TRUMP whales averaging $1.8 million a pop, and crypto holdings that clash with pending legislation. Trump's added at least $620 million to his fortune from crypto in months – talk about executive perks.

 

The Ethical Tightrope

 

Is This Fraud or Just “Business”? Legal eagles are split. Proving insider trading needs “material non-public information,” per Professor Sarah Williams. Former White House ethics lawyer Richard Painter says Trump's “playing with fire,” and the Oxford Law Blog warns of “the most far-reaching securities fraud in history.” No smoking gun yet, even while the smoke is thick enough to choke on.

 

Innovation vs. Opportunism

 

In the end, this saga blurs the line between public service and private empire-building like never before. As a developer who's tinkered with blockchain, I get the innovation appeal – but when it's tied to the presidency, it smells more like opportunism than opportunity. What do you think?

2. Congressional Investigations: Reports from the House Committee on Financial Services on market manipulation and ethics violations.

item.title: Israel's Starvation of Palestine ~ 40,000 Babies At Risk
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
An Objective Glimpse into Israel's Recent War Crimes

Heartbreak is unfolding in Gaza as the Israeli-imposed Palestinian humanitarian crisis takes another chilling turn. Just this week, two more infants became the latest Palestinian children to die from malnutrition. Over 120 people—more than 80 of them children—have now starved to death as Israel’s blockade tightens around the Gaza Strip.

Doctors inside Gaza describe a nightmare: children brought to hospitals weak from hunger. even the doctors themselves, dizzy and malnourished, can barely stand. Some children are being breastfed water instead of formula. Hospitals have no medicines. Fathers and mothers cry at the doors because there’s nothing anyone can do.

The director of Gaza’s main children’s hospital gave a chilling warning: “Children are the group most vulnerable to the famine conditions gripping the territory… There would be mass deaths if border crossings are not immediately opened.”Gaza’s government says 100,000 children aged two and under—including 40,000 babies—are now at risk of dying within days. There is no baby milk, no nutritional supplements, and aid trucks are blocked at the borders. Meanwhile, international leaders from Germany, France, and the UK are urging Israel to lift the blockade and let help reach those who desperately need it.

A Personal Reflection

When faced with these painful realities, I sometimes ask myself and God why we're allowing helpless children to be starved. Why is Israel committing these heinous atrocities, and why is my government sanctioning it?

Why would people who were less than a century ago strong-armed, starved, and dehumanized themselves turn around and commit those same atrocities upon a neighboring people? And while some do periodically come forward to say something, nothing is being done. The world is either pretending it isn't happening or idling, observing on the sidelines while thousands of innocent civilians, including youngsters and babies, are paying for it agonizingly with their lives.

It’s challenging to imagine, but this is reality now for families in Gaza. If we believe in basic humanity, we can’t look away. Share this story. Speak about it. Contact your representatives. We can’t let the world forget Gaza’s children.

item.title: The Epstein Jail Video Pt. 2: The DOJ's Smoking Gun
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
The Official Story (Or, "Nothing to See Here")

Federal officials, including the FBI and DOJ, claimed the video evidence was airtight. They insisted it captured every angle needed to rule out foul play. But a CBS News investigation, released years later, exposes a narrative full of conspiracy-sized holes. This goes to show you that the mainstream media is capable of real investigation when it suits their corporate liberal agenda and could stand to damage or tarnish Trump's credibility.

How "Conspiracy Theories" are Born

Wrong Angles, Wrong Assumptions

The 11-hour video never shows the actual entrance to Epstein's cell or the SHU tier. The staircase leading to his cell? Out of frame. The doors into the unit? Also out of frame. So how did the DOJ conclude definitively that no one entered? CBS digitally reconstructed the layout and found that the camera's field of view could not capture key access points. Which makes the repeated assertion that the footage is definitive... well, definitively misleading.

The Mysterious "Orange Shape"

At 10:40 p.m. - A mysterious orange blur climbs the stairs. DOJ says it was a guard bringing linens. Forensic experts reviewing the footage weren't convinced. It could easily be an inmate. Or a pile of Cheetos. We'll never know.

The Cursor and Menu That Shouldn't Exist

Let's talk about what is quite possibly the biggest red flag. The video included a visible computer cursor and a playback menu. Translation: the video wasn't a DVR export; it was a screen recording. Metadata analysis revealed the file was created in May 2023, not in 2019. Experts believe this means the so-called "raw footage" was screen captured years after the fact. There was also a shift in aspect ratio mid-video, strongly suggesting two clips were spliced together.

The "Missing Minute"

Just before midnight, the timestamp skips ahead by one minute. No explanation. No technical log. Just poof — one minute gone. AG Pam Bondi claimed this was due to an automatic nightly reset. But other DOJ sources confirmed the unedited original does not have a missing minute. So, which is it? Or better yet, why can't we see that version?

Staff Statements That Don't Match the Tape

Tova Noel, a prison official, claimed she left Epstein alone. Video shows her escorting him. Another staffer appears on camera before and after Epstein's final movement. She was never mentioned in the official report. At 12:05 a.m., a third, unidentified person walks through the unit. The Inspector General never addresses this. Meanwhile, Noel and fellow officer Michael Thomas are visible in the common area while other people enter and exit the unit. How? Through two doors that supposedly only they had keys to.

The Unmonitored Call to Epstein's "Mother"

While checking into the prison, Epstein was permitted to make an unmonitored call to his mother, even though she had passed away in 2003 from leukemia. Instead, he called a New York number. A man answered. The call was never recorded. The Bureau of Prisons later admitted they had no idea what was said and no log of the call, clearly defining a breach of protocol.

The Inmates and the Silence

The tier where Epstein was housed included up to 14 inmates. Only three spoke to investigators. Only one was identified publicly. No footage from inside the tier was ever released. Not even a grainy GIF. And yes, two other camera feeds have not been mentioned or released. A still from one camera made it into the DOJ report. Great — a screenshot. That solves everything.

Expert Criticism and Shrugging Bureaucrats

CBS interviewed multiple forensic video experts. All of them had varying comments and concerns, but one thing they all had undoubtedly in common was that this was not the original footage and that it was a screen recording. Even more concerning, experts also agree that it is likely two recordings spliced together to appear like one continuous 11-hour video piece, which we all would have surely fallen for, except whoever edited this either intentionally or very stupidly leaves an editing menu in the upper right corner of the screen at around midnight. This means the footage is unreliable, edited, and incomplete. Robert Hood, former BOP official, called the summary reports inadequate. Even the Bureau's own Northeast director admitted the unmonitored phone call was deeply concerning. Mark Epstein, Jeffrey's brother, continues to assert that his brother was murdered. And frankly, after reading the CBS investigation, it's hard to blame him.

Final Thoughts

This is proving to be an unbelievable and historic failure of accountability surrounding one of the most high-profile prisoners in U.S. custody. Whether by incompetence or intent, the Epstein video fails the most basic standard of evidence: it doesn't show the thing it's supposed to prove. So the next time someone says, "There's video proof he acted alone," feel free to reply: "Cool. Can I see the part where that happens?"

item.title: Tragedy in Gaza: Israeli Forces Kill 62 Palestinians, Many While Seeking Aid
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
Another dark day in Gaza as dozens of civilians, desperate for food, are killed at aid distribution sites.

On Saturday, August 2, 2025, another unfortunate and unnecessary loss of life unfolded in the Gaza Strip as Israeli forces killed 62 Palestinians. The tragedy is compounded by the fact that a significant portion of these deaths occurred among civilians seeking life-saving humanitarian aid, highlighting the severe and ongoing crisis in the region.

According to reports, 38 of the 62 individuals killed lost their lives at aid distribution points managed by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), a U.S. and Israeli-backed organization that is evidently not upholding its title.

Israel's War Crimes Continue

This event is not an isolated one but rather the latest in a disturbing pattern of deadly violence against those trying to access essential supplies. Witnesses and human rights groups have documented a consistent stream of attacks on civilians at aid locations. Since late May 2025 alone, it is reported that at least 1,373 Palestinians have been killed while attempting to get food for their families, either at GHF sites or along the routes of aid convoys.

"Tactical Pauses" Fail to Protect Civilians

These killings have continued despite an announcement by Israel on July 27, 2025, of daily "tactical pauses" in military operations. These pauses were intended to create a safe corridor for humanitarian aid to reach desperate populations, however, the continued violence raises serious questions about their effectiveness and implementation.

Growing International Concerns

The situation has drawn sharp condemnation from the international community. Human Rights Watch has accurately labeled the routine killing of civilians seeking food as "war crimes".

This follows numerous witness accounts from Gaza alleging that Israeli soldiers and associated security contractors have deliberately targeted people at aid sites.

A Deepening Humanitarian Catastrophe

The broader context is one of extreme desperation. The UN human rights office noted that in the two days leading up to this incident (July 30–31), 105 Palestinians were killed and over 680 injured while attempting to gain access to basic necessities.

The humanitarian crisis is spiraling. Gaza's Ministry of Health has reported that 169 Palestinians have died from starvation and malnutrition since the conflict escalated in October 2023, a grim testament to the catastrophic conditions on the ground.

The events of August 2nd are a painful reminder of the human cost of this conflict and the urgent need for a meaningful intervention to protect civilian lives.

item.title: Israeli Security Cabinet's Decision on Gaza
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
Escalation Without Clear Planning

In a move that has sparked international concern and domestic backlash, Israel's security cabinet has approved a plan to take control of Gaza City, signaling a significant escalation in the ongoing conflict. This decision, made during an hours-long meeting, opens the door to further military operations in the Gaza Strip. Still, it comes with substantial risks and a glaring lack of comprehensive planning.

A Risky Escalation

The security cabinet's approval of the plan to occupy Gaza City is a deeply alarming prospect. Critics, including top United Nations officials, have warned that such a move would be against international law and could lead to catastrophic consequences for Palestinian civilians and Israeli hostages still held in Gaza. The World Health Organization has reported that July was the worst month for cases of acute malnutrition in children in Gaza, affecting nearly 12,000 under the age of five, highlighting the already dire humanitarian crisis in the region. Despite these warnings, the Israeli security cabinet, which includes key ministers such as far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, both of whom oppose a Gaza ceasefire deal, pushed forward with the plan. The decision was framed as a necessary step to achieve a decisive victory over Hamas, the group responsible for the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel that triggered the current war.

Lack of Planning and Unintended Consequences

One of the most concerning aspects of this decision is the apparent lack of planning for the aftermath of a military takeover. While the military believes it could seize the remaining parts of Gaza within months, setting up a stable system of governance similar to that in the Israeli-occupied West Bank would require up to five years of sustained combat, according to security officials. This timeline suggests a prolonged period of instability and violence, with no clear strategy for addressing the humanitarian needs of the Palestinian population. Moreover, the decision has been met with fierce criticism from various quarters. Families of hostages held by militants in Gaza have blasted Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a move they say puts hostages' lives at risk. Opposition leaders in Israel have also condemned the plan, arguing that it is a bad operational, moral, and economic idea. International leaders, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and regional power Saudi Arabia, have urged Israel to reconsider its decision, citing the potential for further escalation and the need for a peaceful resolution.

Humanitarian Crisis Deepens

The humanitarian situation in Gaza is already dire, with millions of Palestinians displaced from their homes and forced to live in tents and makeshift shelters. The UN has warned that a complete military takeover would exacerbate this crisis, leading to even greater suffering for the civilian population. The Israeli military's plan to provide humanitarian aid "outside the combat zones" falls short of addressing the systemic issues that have led to the current catastrophe.

Final Thoughts

The Israeli security cabinet's decision to pursue temporary occupation and total control over Gaza is a dangerous gamble with potentially devastating consequences. Without a clear plan for the post-occupation period and amid an ongoing humanitarian crisis, this move risks further escalation involving additional. All parties involved must seek a peaceful resolution that addresses the root causes of the conflict and prioritizes the well-being of civilians on both sides. As the situation evolves, the international community must step up its efforts to broker a ceasefire and support humanitarian aid efforts in Gaza. The path forward must be one of diplomacy and dialogue, not further militarization and occupation.

item.title: The Two-Party System and the Convergence of Power
item.dc:creator: m1stykmedia
item.content:encoded:
A Historical Analysis of Political Co-operation

Introduction

If you’ve spent any time on X (formerly Twitter) lately, then you’ve probably witnessed the political circus firsthand. CNN and Fox News warriors, waving their blue and red flags, hurl the loudest, most offensive memes they can dig up at each other. Users have opted for blood sport in place of constructive debate as each posting is designed to enrage the other side and widen the canyon of political disparity between them. But here’s the uncomfortable truth: it doesn’t matter which side you pick. Yes, you read that correctly. The Democratic and Republican parties are two sides of the same coin—a coin that, no matter how it flips, always ends up in the pockets of the elites who’ve rigged the system against you. It began with a degree of subtlety, but has picked up pace and morphed into an ordeal we can no longer ignore. Call it the American casino. Your vote is the roulette ball, blue and red are your colors, and while you argue over where it lands, the house, i.e., the corporations, lobbyists, military-industrial complex, etc., keeps stacking chips.

The Origins: From No Parties to Two

When the Declaration of Independence (1776) was signed, the Founders hadn’t yet invented political parties. They actively feared them. George Washington’s Farewell Address warned against “the baneful effects of the spirit of party.” James Madison, in Federalist No. 10, called factions dangerous, though he figured a large republic might dilute their power. But ideals collide with reality fast. By the 1790s, factions hardened into the first U.S. parties:
  • Federalists (Hamilton, Adams) → strong central government, pro-commerce.
  • Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson, Madison) → agrarian, states’ rights, pro-France.
By the 1820s, the Federalists collapsed, and a new two-party cycle emerged: Democrats vs. Whigs, then Democrats vs. Republicans by the 1860s. Despite all the warnings, the United States locked itself into a permanent two-party structure in less than a century.

The Historical Timeline (1776 → Today)

  • 1776–1787: No parties. The Revolution united colonists.
  • 1790s: Federalists vs. Democratic-Republicans. Washington hated it, but the split stuck.
  • 1820s–1850s: Democrats (Jacksonian populists) vs. Whigs (pro-business).
  • 1860s: Republicans (Lincoln, anti-slavery, pro-industry) vs. Democrats (pro-slavery South). Civil War entrenched the divide.
  • Late 1800s–1900s: Both parties become vehicles for corporate and industrial power. Gilded Age politics were basically bribery with ballots.
  • 1930s: New Deal Democrats vs. pro-business Republicans. FDR expands government, GOP resists, but both are still tied to donors.
  • 1960s–1980s: Civil Rights shifts party coalitions; Nixon’s “Southern Strategy” rewires the map; Reagan brings corporate deregulation and evangelicals to the GOP; Democrats adapt but don’t uproot the system.
  • 2000s–Today: Culture war polarization goes nuclear—but on war, surveillance, and corporate protection, both sides quietly converge.

Bipartisan Policies: The Great Convergence

Here’s the dirty truth, the X warriors were not informed of: Politicians may don their red and blue jerseys and scream at each other on the podium or on camera, but behind closed doors, they’ve been quietly building the same machine. Different marketing, same product. Here are some examples. Take a look at the Patriot Act. Republicans used to preach about limiting government power, yet under George W. Bush they rammed through one of the most sweeping expansions of federal surveillance in history. Warrantless wiretaps, data dragnets, the works. Then, Obama, the supposed constitutional scholar, kept it alive and even expanded it. Our precious civil liberties in a post 9/11 world were sacrificed on the altar of “security,” regardless of who was in office. Or look at foreign policy. Since 9/11, both parties have treated the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force like a blank check. The invasion of Iraq under false pretenses by Bush, Libya and drone wars under Obama, record defense budgets under Trump, and Biden’s Ukraine and Israeli military aid packages. It doesn’t appear to matter if it’s a cowboy conservative or a polished progressive—the military-industrial complex gets paid either way. Then there’s Wall Street. When the 2008 financial crisis hit, Bush started the bailouts, Obama expanded them, and Congress from both sides signed off. Banks got saved, CEOs kept their bonuses, and regular people got foreclosure notices. Neither party reinstated the safeguards (like Glass-Steagall) that could’ve prevented it in the first place. Even the tax code shows the same hand. Bush slashed taxes for the wealthy, Obama made most of those cuts permanent, Trump doubled down with corporate giveaways, Biden—despite all the campaign talk—did not reverse them. Big Tech, Big Oil, Big Pharma? They all get their subsidies and sweetheart deals no matter who’s smiling in the Oval Office photo ops. And let’s not forget the War on Drugs and mass incarceration. Clinton built the prison boom, Bush escalated the drug war, Obama mostly maintained it, and Biden—who helped draft those “tough on crime” policies—only started pretending to rethink them right towards the end of his term. The prison-industrial complex doesn’t care if the guards wear red ties or blue ties. Now we arrive at Trump’s second term. Instead of reversing course, he has amplified the trend. Not only has he picked up where Biden left off—sustaining surveillance authorities, defense contracts, and corporate protections—he has now taken the unprecedented step of mobilizing military force domestically. In Washington, D.C., Trump federalized local police and brought in National Guard units to “restore order” despite historically low violent crime. In Los Angeles, he deployed troops without the governor’s request, sparking lawsuits and constitutional challenges. What was once a bipartisan consensus around war and surveillance abroad has now crept homeward: military power turned inward on American citizens. To make matters worse, the trump administration has already signed numerous contracts with big tech giants as they seek to further enmesh the private and public sectors to instate what appears to be an autocratic technocracy. Let's be honest with ourselves, do we really think voting for a Democrat next time will slow any of this down?

Final Thoughts: The House Always Wins

So here we are. It's no wonder the founding fathers warned against factionalism. If we don't course correct soon, the results could prove dire for our republic, so there isn't much time. So next time your blood starts boiling over a politically charged internet meme remember: The two-party system that pretends to offer choice really only quietly maintains elite interests. Surveillance continues. Wars continue. Corporate bailouts continue. And now, even the military has been pulled directly into domestic politics. The culture war is the entertainment, the outrage machine that keeps you busy. The real game is happening at the casino table, where the roulette ball spins red or blue, but the house—the corporations, the lobbyists, the military-industrial complex—always wins. Today, the only difference is that the casino’s guards are no longer just protecting the table. They’re walking the streets of Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. -MiStyk
